Arc 1: Mathematical & Computational Prerequisites

Optimizers: Momentum, Adam, and Learning Rate Schedules

12 min readbuilds on Gradients and How Machines Learn

A note on this series

I built this series as a learning project and used Claude extensively for research, drafting, critique, coding, and revision. I chose the curriculum and dependency order, drove the questions, edited the explanations, developed the interactive examples, and take responsibility for the published result.

This is an educational first edition rather than a formal reference. I am reviewing the articles against primary sources, testing the executable examples, and tracking corrections as the series matures. Some examples require specific hardware, model weights, or external services; they are teaching examples, not a tested deployment recipe.

SGDMomentumAdamx² + 10y²

Three update rules on the same bowl, with separately chosen learning rates: SGD 0.085, momentum 0.012, Adam 0.18. These paths illustrate the rules, not a performance ranking.

In the last post, we got gradient descent working. We computed gradients, applied the chain rule backwards through a network, and updated parameters with a simple rule: θ←θ−η∇L\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta \nabla Lθ←θ−η∇L. In stochastic gradient descent, we estimate that gradient from a sampled batch.

A single learning rate can make progress slow when the loss curves sharply in one direction and gently in another.

We will use a narrow valley to compare momentum, adaptive scaling, and AdamW, then put together a learning-rate schedule.

The problem with vanilla SGD

Imagine you're walking down a long, skinny valley. The walls are steep, but the floor slopes gently toward the minimum at the far end. SGD bounces back and forth between the steep walls while barely making progress along the floor. Each step overshoots in the steep direction and undershoots in the shallow one.

Loss curvature can vary substantially across directions in parameter space. SGD multiplies every gradient coordinate by the same learning rate, so that rate must accommodate the steep directions.

If you set the learning rate high enough to make progress in the flat direction, you'll overshoot and oscillate in the steep direction. Set it low enough to be stable in the steep direction, and you'll crawl along the valley floor slowly.

Here's what that looks like. The surface below is f(x,y)=x2+10y2f(x,y) = x^2 + 10y^2f(x,y)=x2+10y2, an elongated bowl where the yyy-direction is ten times steeper than the xxx-direction. Watch SGD bounce:

The same bowl and starting point, with separately chosen learning rates: SGD 0.08, momentum 0.01, Adam 0.15. Compare update paths, not a controlled speed benchmark.

SGD alternates across the valley; momentum carries information from previous gradients; Adam also scales each coordinate using recent squared gradients.

Momentum

Vanilla SGD uses only the current gradient. Momentum accumulates a running velocity, so earlier gradients continue to influence the next update.

The velocity vector vvv accumulates past gradients:

vt=β⋅vt−1+∇L(θt)v_t = \beta \cdot v_{t-1} + \nabla L(\theta_t)vt​=β⋅vt−1​+∇L(θt​) θt+1=θt−η⋅vt\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \cdot v_tθt+1​=θt​−η⋅vt​

The hyperparameter β\betaβ (typically 0.9) controls how much of the previous velocity we retain. When β=0\beta = 0β=0, this is just vanilla SGD. When β=0.9\beta = 0.9β=0.9, gradients roughly ten steps back still contribute. This velocity is an unnormalized weighted sum; multiplying it by 1−β1-\beta1−β would give an exponential moving average.

In a direction where gradients alternate sign, their contributions to velocity can partly cancel. Where they consistently point the same way, they accumulate. The learning rate and momentum coefficient determine whether this improves progress or produces further overshoot.

Side by side, here are the two arrows that matter at every step. On the left, vanilla SGD: the descent direction is just −∇L-\nabla L−∇L, which flips wildly across the valley walls. On the right, momentum computes the gradient at its own position (faint red) but updates use −v-v−v (blue), which averages out the oscillation and points roughly along the floor:

Each ball evaluates the gradient at its own location. The blue arrow includes the accumulated velocity; the red arrow uses the current gradient alone.

Polyak introduced momentum in 1964; Chapter 8 of Deep Learning develops its connection to a damped physical system.

Per-parameter adaptive rates: RMSProp

Momentum still uses a single learning rate. RMSProp additionally rescales each coordinate using its recent gradient magnitudes.

Hinton presented RMSProp in his 2012 Coursera lectures. It tracks a running average of squared gradients:

st=β⋅st−1+(1−β)⋅(∇L)2s_t = \beta \cdot s_{t-1} + (1 - \beta) \cdot (\nabla L)^2st​=β⋅st−1​+(1−β)⋅(∇L)2

Then divide the update by st\sqrt{s_t}st​​:

θt+1=θt−ηst+ϵ⋅∇L(θt)\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \frac{\eta}{\sqrt{s_t} + \epsilon} \cdot \nabla L(\theta_t)θt+1​=θt​−st​​+ϵη​⋅∇L(θt​)

Parameters with consistently large gradients get their effective learning rate shrunk. Parameters with consistently small gradients get their effective learning rate boosted. The ϵ\epsilonϵ (usually 10−810^{-8}10−8) prevents division by zero and also affects updates when the denominator is small.

sts_tst​ has units of squared gradient. Taking st\sqrt{s_t}st​​ puts the denominator on the gradient scale, so gt/stg_t / \sqrt{s_t}gt​/st​​ compares the current gradient with recent magnitudes.

Adam: combining the two moments

Adam, introduced by Kingma and Ba in 2014, combines first- and second-moment estimates.

It maintains two running averages:

  • First moment mtm_tmt​: a running average of the gradients (like momentum's velocity)
  • Second moment vtv_tvt​: a running average of the squared gradients (like RMSProp's denominator)
mt=β1⋅mt−1+(1−β1)⋅gtm_t = \beta_1 \cdot m_{t-1} + (1 - \beta_1) \cdot g_tmt​=β1​⋅mt−1​+(1−β1​)⋅gt​ vt=β2⋅vt−1+(1−β2)⋅gt2v_t = \beta_2 \cdot v_{t-1} + (1 - \beta_2) \cdot g_t^2vt​=β2​⋅vt−1​+(1−β2​)⋅gt2​

There's one wrinkle. Both mmm and vvv are initialized at zero. In the early steps, they're biased toward zero because they haven't accumulated enough history. Adam corrects for this with a bias correction step:

m^t=mt1−β1t,v^t=vt1−β2t\hat{m}_t = \frac{m_t}{1 - \beta_1^t}, \quad \hat{v}_t = \frac{v_t}{1 - \beta_2^t}m^t​=1−β1t​mt​​,v^t​=1−β2t​vt​​

Then the update is:

θt+1=θt−η⋅m^tv^t+ϵ\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \cdot \frac{\hat{m}_t}{\sqrt{\hat{v}_t} + \epsilon}θt+1​=θt​−η⋅v^t​​+ϵm^t​​

Common defaults are β1=0.9\beta_1 = 0.9β1​=0.9, β2=0.999\beta_2 = 0.999β2​=0.999, and ϵ=10−8\epsilon = 10^{-8}ϵ=10−8; their suitability depends on the run.

This example compares two proportional gradient histories: A's values are around 5 and B's are A's divided by 100. In Adam's update η⋅m^/(v^+ϵ)\eta \cdot \hat{m} / (\sqrt{\hat{v}} + \epsilon)η⋅m^/(v^​+ϵ), this scale factor cancels between the numerator and denominator apart from epsilon. The resulting step sizes are similar despite the different raw gradients.

A worked Adam step

For three consecutive steps on a single parameter, let θ\thetaθ start at 1.0 and use gradients 0.5, 0.4, and 0.6. We use η = 0.1, β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.999, and ε = 10⁻⁸:

On step 1, the raw m1=0.1⋅0.5=0.05m_1 = 0.1 \cdot 0.5 = 0.05m1​=0.1⋅0.5=0.05, but m^1=0.05/(1−0.9)=0.5\hat{m}_1 = 0.05 / (1 - 0.9) = 0.5m^1​=0.05/(1−0.9)=0.5. The second moment is corrected the same way: v1=0.001⋅0.25=0.00025v_1 = 0.001 \cdot 0.25 = 0.00025v1​=0.001⋅0.25=0.00025, but v^1=0.00025/(1−0.999)=0.25\hat{v}_1 = 0.00025 / (1 - 0.999) = 0.25v^1​=0.00025/(1−0.999)=0.25. Both corrections work together; they're not redundant. Correcting only mmm would make the first update about 31.6η31.6\eta31.6η, too large relative to η\etaη; correcting only vvv would make it 0.1η0.1\eta0.1η, too small, because v1≈0.0158\sqrt{v_1} \approx 0.0158v1​​≈0.0158 is much smaller than v^1=0.5\sqrt{\hat{v}_1} = 0.5v^1​​=0.5 in the denominator.

The two correction factors fade at different rates. The mmm-correction 1/(1−β1t)1/(1-\beta_1^t)1/(1−β1t​) with β1=0.9\beta_1 = 0.9β1​=0.9 becomes negligible within a hundred steps or so. The vvv-correction 1/(1−β2t)1/(1-\beta_2^t)1/(1−β2t​) with β2=0.999\beta_2 = 0.999β2​=0.999 takes much longer: at t=100t=100t=100 it's still about 1/0.095≈10.51/0.095 \approx 10.51/0.095≈10.5, and even at t=1000t=1000t=1000 it's about 1/0.632≈1.581/0.632 \approx 1.581/0.632≈1.58. Bias correction matters for thousands of steps for the second moment, not just the first few.

AdamW: decoupled weight decay

When training neural networks, you almost always want some form of regularization to prevent overfitting. The most common is weight decay, where you gently shrink selected weights toward zero (biases and normalization parameters are often excluded). In vanilla SGD, weight decay and L2 regularization are mathematically equivalent: adding λθ\lambda \thetaλθ to the gradient is the same as adding λ2∥θ∥2\frac{\lambda}{2} \|\theta\|^22λ​∥θ∥2 to the loss.

In Adam, adding the L2 term to the gradient also changes the first- and second-moment estimates. That produces a different update from shrinking the parameters directly. AdamW separates these operations so the decay term does not pass through the moment estimates.

Loshchilov and Hutter (2017) pointed this out and proposed AdamW, which decouples the weight decay from the gradient-based update:

θt+1=θt−η(m^tv^t+ϵ+λθt)\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \left( \frac{\hat{m}_t}{\sqrt{\hat{v}_t} + \epsilon} + \lambda \theta_t \right)θt+1​=θt​−η(v^t​​+ϵm^t​​+λθt​)

The weight decay term λθt\lambda \theta_tλθt​ shrinks parameters directly, outside Adam's moment scaling. An optimizer described as "Adam" may implement this decoupled form or apply L2 regularization through the gradient; inspect the update rule when reproducing a training recipe.

Learning rate schedules: warmup + cosine decay

A learning-rate schedule changes the size of updates during training. Warmup limits the initial steps; decay makes later updates smaller.

Warmup

Large initial updates can destabilize training before the optimizer has useful gradient statistics. Warmup reduces these early updates while those statistics and the model activations change.

The fix is simple: start with a very small learning rate and linearly increase it to your target over the first NNN warmup steps.

ηt=ηmax⋅tTwarmupfor t≤Twarmup\eta_t = \eta_{\text{max}} \cdot \frac{t}{T_{\text{warmup}}} \quad \text{for } t \leq T_{\text{warmup}}ηt​=ηmax​⋅Twarmup​t​for t≤Twarmup​

The warmup length is a hyperparameter, not a fixed percentage. The original LLaMA paper used 2,000 warmup steps. The right choice depends on the model, batch size, and peak learning rate.

Cosine decay

A decay phase gradually reduces the learning rate toward a chosen minimum. One common choice is cosine decay:

ηt=ηmin+12(ηmax−ηmin)(1+cos⁡(t−TwarmupTtotal−Twarmup⋅π))\eta_t = \eta_{\text{min}} + \frac{1}{2}(\eta_{\text{max}} - \eta_{\text{min}}) \left(1 + \cos\left(\frac{t - T_{\text{warmup}}}{T_{\text{total}} - T_{\text{warmup}}} \cdot \pi\right)\right)ηt​=ηmin​+21​(ηmax​−ηmin​)(1+cos(Ttotal​−Twarmup​t−Twarmup​​⋅π))

It traces a smooth half-cosine from ηmax\eta_{\text{max}}ηmax​ down to ηmin\eta_{\text{min}}ηmin​ (often set to something like 0.1×ηmax0.1 \times \eta_{\text{max}}0.1×ηmax​ or even zero). It decays slowly at first, accelerates in the middle, and slows down near the end.

Here is the whole schedule end to end. The dot rides through 30k steps: a fast linear ramp during the first 10% of training (warmup, amber), then a smooth cosine descent down toward ηmin\eta_\text{min}ηmin​ (decay, blue):

An illustrative 30k-step schedule with 3k warmup steps. The dot marks the current step.

The cosine schedule appeared in work on warm restarts and was later used in Chinchilla and LLaMA training. It requires a chosen decay horizon. Warmup-Stable-Decay schedules instead keep a stable phase and begin a cooldown when training is nearing its end.

What this costs at scale

Adam and AdamW store two moment tensors, mmm and vvv, with one entry per parameter. With fp32 moments, that is 8 bytes per parameter, in addition to weights, gradients, and activations.

For a 7B parameter model stored in fp32 (4 bytes per parameter), the model weights take 28 GB. The optimizer state takes another 56 GB. For a 70B model? 280 GB of weights plus 560 GB of optimizer state. This is why training large models requires so much more memory than inference, even before you account for gradients and activations.

With bf16 weights (2 bytes per parameter), two fp32 moment tensors occupy four times as many bytes as the weights. An optional fp32 master-weight copy adds another 4 bytes per parameter. The exact allocation depends on the training implementation. ZeRO can shard these states across devices, and low-bit optimizers reduce their storage precision.

Common misconceptions

"Adam always beats SGD." Results depend on the objective, tuning, data, and compute budget. AdamW is a common transformer optimizer, but that convention is not a guarantee of better convergence or generalization.

"Learning rate is the only hyperparameter that matters." Warmup, weight decay, clipping, and the beta values affect the updates too. For example, a lower β₂ makes the second-moment estimate respond more quickly to changing gradients. Their useful values depend on the training run.

"One recipe works for every transformer." AdamW with warmup and cosine decay is a useful recipe to understand. Peak learning rate, batch size, decay, clipping, betas, and the schedule still need evaluation for the actual run. Other optimizers and schedules make different memory and convergence tradeoffs.

What's next

We have a training loop and several ways to turn a gradient into a parameter update. The next question is how to store and compute those updates when memory and arithmetic precision are limited.

The next post is GPUs, Floating Point, and Why Precision Matters: what fp32, bf16, and fp8 represent, and why training combines formats.
